5-5.title: Use Partial Products to Multiply Multi-Digit Factors

questions.title: Be Curious · What do you notice? What do you wonder?
questions.hint: Compare the numbers inside the area model with the numbers in the list on the right.
steps: Look at the area model: 374 is split into 300 + 70 + 4 and 43 into 40 + 3.
Find each box's number in the list on the right (12,000 is 40 × 300, and so on).
Say what you notice, then ask a question you wonder about.
questions.answer: Sample answer: I notice both show 374 × 43. The six numbers in the area model are the same six partial products in the list, and they add to 16,082. I wonder if this works for any two numbers.
questions.verification: Computed 374 × 43 = 16,082 in Python and summed the six printed partial products (12,000 + 2,800 + 160 + 900 + 210 + 12 = 16,082).

questions.title: Math is… Mindset

steps: Think about what helps you pay attention.

questions.title: Learn · Seats in the stadium
questions.hint: Each of the 164 rows has 82 seats, so multiply 164 × 82.

questions.title: Math is… Generalizations
questions.hint: Each box in an area model is one partial product.
steps: Picture 164 × 82 as a rectangle split into parts.
Each small rectangle's area is one partial product.
Adding all the small areas gives the whole area, the product.
questions.answer: Sample answer: The area model splits the big rectangle into smaller boxes. Each box is one partial product, and adding the boxes gives the total, just like adding the partial products in the vertical list.
questions.verification: Original source visually checked; open-ended prompt, sample answer reviewed for accuracy.

questions.title: Work Together · 142 × 63
steps: Line up the partial products vertically and add them.
questions.verification: Computed 142 × 63 = 8,946 in Python; checked partial-product sum and estimate 140 × 60 = 8,400.

questions.title: Problem 1 · 325 × 73

questions.title: Problem 2 · 104 × 28
questions.hint: 32 is 8 × 4 and 800 is 8 × 100; now multiply by the 20.

questions.title: Problem 3 · 17 × 86
questions.verification: Computed 17 × 86 = 1,462 in Python; partial products 800 + 560 + 60 + 42; estimate 20 × 80 = 1,600.

questions.title: Problem 4 · 24 × 129

questions.title: 11 · Raya's error
questions.hint: Compare the top number in Raya's work with the problem, 128 × 17.
steps: Raya's partial products come from 200 + 10 + 8 = 218, not 128, so her total is wrong.
Add them to get the correct product.
questions.verification: Read from the page: the problem is 128 × 17; Raya's printed work starts with 208 and her partial products add to 3,706 = 218 × 17. Computed 128 × 17 = 2,176 in Python and by partial products.

questions.title: 12 · Extend Your Thinking · 384 × 725
questions.hint: Split 384 into 300 + 80 + 4 and 725 into 700 + 20 + 5; you get nine partial products.
questions.answer: 278,400. Multiplying each place-value part of 384 by each part of 725 gives nine partial products whose sum is 278,400.
questions.verification: Computed 384 × 725 = 278,400 in Python; sum of nine partial products also 278,400; checked 384 × 725 = 384 × 29 × 25 = 11,136 × 25 = 278,400.

questions.title: Reflect · Partial products
questions.hint: Think about how you broke apart the factors on this page.
steps: Split each factor by place value.
Multiply every part of one factor by every part of the other.
questions.answer: Sample answer: I break each factor into hundreds, tens and ones, multiply each part of one factor by each part of the other, then add all the partial products to get the product.
